name: Syntactic Tree Depth Variance
description: Analyzes the distribution of parse tree depths across a document. When sentences are diagrammed into hierarchical syntactic trees, the 'depth' represents how many layers of nested clauses or modifications exist. Research (Jawahar et al., 2020) demonstrates that Large Language Models stubbornly produce texts with a rigidly uniform, 'safe' tree depth. They avoid both extremely shallow fragments and deeply convoluted, multi-layered human sentences, resulting in a statistically anomalous lack of depth variance.
mechanism: The algorithm parses every sentence into a formal constituency tree and measures its maximum vertical depth from the root node to the deepest 'leaf' (word). It then plots the distribution of these depths across the entire text. If the variance (standard deviation) of the tree depths is unusually low—meaning almost every sentence has the exact same structural 'height'—the text is flagged as a mathematically optimized product of a neural network rather than natural human composition.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing formal reports, essays, and articles where human writers naturally mix short, punchy statements (shallow trees) with expansive, detailed explanations (deep trees).
strengths:
• Detects the fundamental mathematical 'safety' of AI generation, which is nearly impossible for a prompter to manually override.
• Highly resistant to basic obfuscation techniques like vocabulary swapping, which do not alter the underlying tree geometry.
limitations:
• Requires computationally heavy constituency parsing for every sentence.
• May flag highly formulaic human writing (e.g., standard operating procedures or specific legal boilerplate) where rigid syntactic uniformity is enforced.
parameters:
Analysis: Constituency Parsing
Metric: Tree Depth Variance (Standard Deviation of Maximum Node Depth)
Output: 0-100 Syntactic Uniformity (Algorithmic Rigidity) Score
accuracy: High — 78-85% standalone accuracy on sufficiently long texts. Excellent when combined with sentence length variance.

references.title: Jawahar, G. et al. (2020). Automatic Detection of Machine Generated Text: A Critical Survey. COLING.
Gibson, E. (1998). Linguistic Complexity: Locality of Syntactic Dependencies. Cognition.
